title: The Power of Not Knowing
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli (in collaboration with Bella of My Ph.Diary) presents Edgar Schein's humble inquiry as a practical skill: asking genuine, open questions free of hidden assumptions or agendas. She argues that professional life trains us to project certainty, and that pre-loaded questions steer people toward the answer they think we want. She offers four concrete shifts, from confirming to discovering, admitting uncertainty, inviting elaboration without guiding it, and naming discomfort. Most examples come from research settings such as interviews, fieldwork, the lab and mentoring, but she extends the practice to leadership, user research, team conversations and conflict. The central move is from being the expert who extracts answers to a learner who seeks understanding.
points: Questions often arrive pre-loaded with assumptions, so people adapt their answers to the expected one and leaders get superficial insight.
Four shifts make humble inquiry practical: confirm less and discover more, admit uncertainty, invite elaboration without guiding it, and name discomfort.
Reframing a leader's question from Are you on track to What do you need from me to succeed implies support and shared responsibility.
In mentoring, asking rather than telling moves the dynamic from top-down to mutual learning and builds the mentee's independence.
The approach has limits: it suits ambiguous situations involving people and trade-offs, not a pilot landing a plane.
quotes: We have been conditioned to project certainty, expertise and control. But admitting you don't know something often unlocks the richest insights.

This is the essence of what Edgar Schein calls humble inquiry: the deliberate practice of asking genuine, curious and open questions, free from hidden assumptions or agendas. Rather than confirming what you already suspect, humble inquiry embraces uncertainty to create space for deeper truths.

What happens in many cases is that questions can unintentionally place others on a predetermined path. People sense what the "right" answer is supposed to be, and they adapt accordingly, often without even realising it.
Instead of asking "How stressful was the recent restructuring?" try "What was your experience during the restructuring?" The former assumes stress, while the latter invites storytelling.

Humble inquiry in the lab means resisting the urge to diagnose problems too quickly and instead creating a space where thoughtful troubleshooting can emerge. It’s especially powerful during technical or experimental challenges, where stress or uncertainty can easily shut down open dialogue.

Through active listening, mentors can spot the moments when a mentee is on the verge of deeper insight and make space for it to emerge. This doesn’t just mean hearing the words, but tuning into tone, hesitation or the questions behind the questions.

You move from being the expert who extracts answers to becoming a learner actively seeking understanding. This shift doesn’t diminish your expertise; rather, it elevates your ability to empathise and engage with people on a deeper level.
